screens.narratorSegment: We begin by framing why careful planning matters when moving systems to the cloud. A migration is not just copying servers; it is an opportunity to reduce long-term costs, improve agility, and remove technical debt. In this lesson you will learn how to discover and inventory an on-premises portfolio, run a meaningful total cost of ownership analysis, and choose the right migration approach using the six Rs: Rehost, Replatform, Refactor, Repurchase, Retain, and Retire. A common misconception is that cloud migration always reduces license costs; in reality software licensing often follows vendor rules and must be evaluated separately. By the end you will be able to justify a migration using objective metrics, pick an appropriate R for each application, and draft a phased plan that aligns technical moves with organizational change management. How confident would you be to start mapping your own portfolio after this chapter?

Each objective emphasizes measurable outcomes: readiness scores, a quantified TCO, an R-strategy across the portfolio, and a discovery dataset that supports wave planning. screens.title: Portfolio Discovery: inventory and dependency mapping
screens.narratorSegment: A practical migration starts with portfolio discovery. Discovery is the process of identifying every application, its servers, databases, and the communication paths between them. You should gather configuration, utilization, and network dependency data so you can form groups of systems that must move together. For example, if an application server repeatedly communicates with a database server on nonstandard ports, those two should be in the same migration wave. Common tools automate collection of C P U, memory, disk, and open connections, which reduces manual inventory errors. A frequent misconception is that discovery only inventories servers; in reality useful discovery includes application owners, business criticality, and compliance constraints. This extra context often drives strategy choice: a high-compliance app may be retained temporarily. Practical steps include running automated collectors, validating discovered dependencies with app owners, and producing a dependency map that feeds wave planning. Example artifact: a CSV row per server with owner, role, resource utilization, and top outbound peers. Key takeaway: accurate discovery shrinks risk and shortens cutover windows. How will you verify dependency accuracy in your next discovery run? Portfolio Discovery: inventory and dependency mapping means inventory and dependency maps reveal grouping constraints and owner context that drive realistic waves and cutover plans.. In practical terms, collect the data that drives every migration decision. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Portfolio Discovery
Process Flow

Inventory → Dependency Map → Validation

Start with an automated inventory that lists servers, databases, and storage. Enrich each item with owner, criticality, and compliance flags.

Collect runtime metrics and network peers to build a dependency map. Identify high-traffic links and grouped components that must migrate together.

Validate findings with application owners to confirm non-obvious dependencies and to capture business constraints.

Example artifact
CSV rows with server, role, owner, CPU avg, memory avg, and top outbound peers.
Common mistake
Trusting a single automated pass; always validate with owners and logs to catch transient dependencies.
Key Takeaway

Discovery must include runtime network data and owner validation to form safe migration waves.

Simulated Discovery Output
# discovery-report.csv
server01,hr-app,owner:hr-app-team,cpu:12%,mem:34%,peers:[db01:1521,auth01:443]
server02,ecom-front,owner:web-team,cpu:45%,mem:60%,peers:[db02:3306,cache01:6379]
db01,oracle-db,owner:db-team,cpu:18%,mem:72%,peers:[server01:1521]
file01,fileshare,owner:it,cpu:5%,mem:12%,peers:[]
How to use this output
  • Group servers with mutual peers for coordinated migration waves.
  • Flag systems with high memory or CPU for sizing estimations in TCO.
  • Record owners and compliance tags before planning cutovers.

screens.title: AWS discovery tooling and what to collect
screens.narratorSegment: Automated discovery tools collect a set of configuration and runtime metrics that are essential for planning. Typical data includes hardware configuration, installed software, C P U and memory utilization, disk usage patterns, and open network connections between hosts. The value of each metric lies in planning and risk reduction: utilization metrics determine right-sizing estimates for cloud instances, while network peers reveal groups that must move together to prevent runtime failures. The chapter references AWS Application Discovery Service and third-party tools as sources of automated collection. Use discovery to answer concrete questions: which servers communicate most often, which servers have single points of failure, and which systems have compliance constraints that prevent immediate migration. A common misconception is relying only on peak utilization; instead use typical and 95th-percentile metrics to size cloud resources practically. Example action: export a dependency map and mark nodes that require synchronous cutover. Final takeaway: discovery transforms assumptions into measurable evidence. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Discovery Tooling
Definition

What discovery tools capture

Configuration: CPU, memory, disk sizes, installed packages and OS versions for inventory and licensing checks.

Utilization: average and peak CPU, memory, and I/O to inform right-sizing and savings potential.

Network peers: outbound and inbound connections to identify coupled systems that should move together.

Why it matters
Peers reveal migration groupings; utilization informs instance sizing and reserved instance planning.
Misconception
Assuming peak utilization equals required cloud size can cause overspend; use typical and percentile metrics.
Simulated discovery snippet
# discovery-sample.json
{
  "server":"ecom-front",
  "cpu_avg":12,
  "cpu_95pct":46,
  "mem_avg":38,
  "disk_io":120,
  "peers":[{"host":"db02","port":3306},{"host":"cache01","port":6379}],
  "owner":"web-team",
  "compliance":"standard"
}
Use this output to
  • Decide whether to right-size compute or consider managed services for databases.
  • Flag synchronous peer groups to migrate together or to use cross-region strategies carefully.
  • Estimate data transfer and cutover approaches based on I/O and peer volume.

screens.title: Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)
screens.narratorSegment: Total Cost of Ownership is a structured way to compare on-premises costs to the cloud across the lifecycle of systems. TCO goes beyond hardware price tags to include power, cooling, datacenter space, software licensing, operational labor for patching and backups, and real estate. When you prepare a TCO for migration, include OpEx versus CapEx shifts and quantify the cost of inaction — missed opportunities that accrue when teams cannot move fast. A common pitfall is failing to capture labor accurately: on-premises labor for routine maintenance often drops when using managed cloud services, but cloud labor shifts toward automation and platform work that still requires skilled staff. Another pitfall is assuming licensing always falls with migration; many vendors require BYOL or new terms. A practical example: move a self-managed database to a managed database service to reduce patching labor, yet account for potential licensing changes. Key takeaway: document assumptions and run sensitivity scenarios so stakeholders see the range of outcomes rather than a single point estimate. What assumption in your current budget would change the most in a cloud model? Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) means include direct costs, operational labor, licensing, and the cost of inaction; run sensitivity scenarios against key assumptions.. In practical terms, a holistic financial view beyond hardware sticker price. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Total Cost of Ownership
Definition

What to include in a migration TCO

Direct costs: hardware, leases, and capital replacement cycles.

Operational costs: staff labor for patching, backups, monitoring, and incident response.

Software licensing: vendor-specific rules may persist in cloud or require alternative approaches.

Facility costs: power, cooling, rack space, and real-estate overheads that cloud removes.

Practical example
Moving a self-managed database to a managed service reduces patching labor but may change licensing and monthly fees.
Common error
Forgetting the cost of new cloud skills and migration project labor inflates expected savings.
TCO worksheet snapshot
  • List baseline on-prem costs by category.
  • Estimate cloud alternatives, include ongoing costs and one-time migration effort.
  • Run sensitivity for labor and licensing assumptions.
Key Takeaway

A robust TCO is transparent about assumptions and tests the impact of licensing and labor changes.

screens.title: The 6 Rs explained
screens.narratorSegment: The six Rs provide a structured vocabulary to decide what to do with each application. Rehost is the lift-and-shift move where systems are moved as-is, often using server replication tools. Replatform involves small optimizations, like moving a self-managed database to a managed database service, without changing the application core. Refactor or re-architect means redesigning the app, perhaps into microservices or serverless, to fully leverage cloud services. Repurchase is replacing an application with a SaaS solution. Retain means leaving applications on-premises for now due to compliance, hardware dependencies, or cost reasons. Retire removes unused applications to reduce scope. A frequent misconception is treating these as strictly exclusive; in practice an application can move through multiple Rs over time — for example, rehost first, then refactor later. Concrete example: a legacy payroll app with strict compliance and no dev team is often rehosted initially, then replatformed or refactored in a later phase. Key takeaway: choose the R that balances risk, cost, and business urgency, and document the rationale so waves are defensible. Which application in your portfolio might follow a stepwise R progression?

keyIdea.title: R is a strategy choice, not a one-time label
keyIdea.text: Document why you chose an R and plan for future transitions when possible, such as rehost followed by refactor.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › The 6 Rs

Strategy cards

Rehost (Lift-and-Shift)
Fastest path; move as-is to cloud compute. Good for urgent or hard-to-change systems.
Replatform
Make small cloud optimizations such as managed databases or platform services.
Refactor
Re-architect to leverage cloud-native services; highest benefit and cost.
Repurchase
Replace with SaaS where appropriate to reduce customization and operational overhead.
Retain
Keep on-premises for regulatory, hardware, or timing reasons; revisit regularly.
Retire
Decommission unused systems to shrink migration scope and cost.
Decision factors
  • Technical complexity and interdependencies
  • Business criticality and acceptable downtime
  • Compliance and hardware requirements
  • Available budget and team capacity
Example: Legacy HR System
Critical, tightly coupled to directory and Oracle, no dev team — often Rehost initially, then plan for future refactor or repurchase.
Note: document the reason for each R decision so stakeholders can revisit strategy as cloud skills and budgets change.

screens.title: Rehost in practice: lift-and-shift
screens.narratorSegment: Rehosting is frequently the right short-term choice for legacy systems that are critical or lack maintainers. The idea is to move systems as-is to cloud compute with minimal application changes, preserving functionality while removing hardware dependency. A practical example is using server replication to produce a target server in the cloud and cut over when ready. AWS provides migration services that can replicate block-level data to speed this path. The primary advantages are speed and reduced immediate risk of introducing application bugs. The trade-offs are that you may carry inefficient architecture into the cloud and miss cloud-native benefits. A common misconception is that rehosting eliminates long-term costs immediately; in many cases you replace CapEx with cloud OpEx while still incurring licensing and maintenance. Best practice: pair rehosting with a medium-term plan to replatform or refactor high-value systems once teams have cloud experience. Key question: which systems are so urgent that a controlled rehost is the best first step? Rehost in practice: lift-and-shift means use lift-and-shift to reduce hardware risk quickly, but document a medium-term plan for optimization or refactor.. In practical terms, when speed and risk avoidance matter most. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Rehost (Lift-and-Shift)

What Rehost is

Move applications as-is to cloud compute to reduce immediate hardware and datacenter risk.

Typical use cases
Legacy apps without active development teams, urgent hardware refreshes, or tight schedules.
Risks and trade-offs
You may preserve inefficient architecture and miss cloud-native cost savings unless a follow-up plan exists.
Scenario Example
A mission-critical payroll system running on a decade-old server is rehosted using block-level replication to minimize downtime. The team plans a later phase to replatform to a managed database and containerize services for better agility.
Key Takeaway

Rehost is a pragmatic first step when speed and operational continuity outweigh immediate modernization benefits.

screens.title: Replatform and Refactor: trade-offs and examples
screens.narratorSegment: Replatform and refactor represent two levels of investment with different paybacks. Replatform, sometimes called lift-tinker-and-shift, means moving to the cloud while making small optimizations. An example is migrating a self-managed relational database to a managed database service, which reduces patching and operational overhead without changing the app. Refactor, however, means re-architecting the application to exploit cloud-native patterns like serverless functions or container orchestration. Refactoring delivers the highest agility and operational cost benefits but requires significant development effort and testing. A misconception is that refactoring always delivers immediate cost savings; often it delivers operational agility and feature velocity, with cost benefits appearing later. Choose replatform when lower risk and quicker outcomes are needed; choose refactor when the app's roadmap demands scalability or continuous delivery improvements. Example: an e-commerce frontend with bursty traffic may be replatformed onto autoscaling managed services, then refactored into microservices as the team invests in cloud-native engineering. Key takeaway: match investment to business value and capacity to change. Replatform and Refactor: trade-offs and examples means replatform for operational relief and speed; refactor to gain long-term agility and cloud-native benefits when justified by roadmap and value.. In practical terms, when to optimize and when to re-architect. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Replatform and refactor represent two levels of investment with different paybacks. Replatform, sometimes called lift-tinker-and-shift, means moving to the cloud while making small optimizations. An example is migrating a self-managed relational database to a managed database service, which reduces patching and operational overhead without changing the app. Refactor, however, means re-architecting the application to exploit cloud-native patterns like serverless functions or container orchestration. Refactoring delivers the highest agility and operational cost benefits but requires significant development effort and testing. A misconception is that refactoring always delivers immediate cost savings; often it delivers operational agility and feature velocity, with cost benefits appearing later. Choose replatform when lower risk and quicker outcomes are needed; choose refactor when the app's roadmap demands scalability or continuous delivery improvements. Example: an e-commerce frontend with bursty traffic may be replatformed onto autoscaling managed services, then refactored into microservices as the team invests in cloud-native engineering. Key takeaway: match investment to business value and capacity to change. Replatform and Refactor: trade-offs and examples means replatform for operational relief and speed; refactor to gain long-term agility and cloud-native benefits when justified by roadmap and value.. In practical terms, when to optimize and when to re-architect. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Optimize according to value
keyIdea.text: Replatform for operational relief and speed; refactor to gain long-term agility and cloud-native benefits when justified by roadmap and value.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Replatform & Refactor

Replatform

Small, targeted changes that adapt systems to managed services or platform features without full redesign.
Example
Move a self-managed MySQL to a managed relational service to reduce operational tasks.
When to choose
When you want faster wins with moderate change risk.

Refactor

Re-architect the application to use cloud primitives like serverless, managed queues, and microservices for scale and velocity.
Example
Break a monolith into services that can scale independently and be deployed with CI/CD pipelines.
Misconception
Refactor is not always cheaper; measure expected velocity and operational savings against rework cost.
Key Takeaway

Choose replatform for quick wins; refactor when roadmap and value justify higher effort and change.

screens.title: Migration Readiness, CCoE, and organizational change
screens.narratorSegment: Technical moves succeed only when people and processes are prepared. A Migration Readiness Assessment evaluates business, people, process, platform, security, and operations readiness for cloud adoption. A Cloud Center of Excellence, or CCoE, centralizes best practices, governance, and tooling. The CCoE provides templates, runbooks, and training so teams can operate in the cloud reliably. Organizational change management includes upskilling engineers, adjusting operational roles from infrastructure maintenance to platform engineering, and communicating cutover windows and rollback procedures to stakeholders. A common mistake is treating migration as a one-time project rather than a transformation that alters runbooks and responsibilities. Example: a monitoring runbook must be updated to use cloud-native alerts and logging; otherwise incident response degrades post-migration. Practical actions include establishing success criteria, training plans, and appointing application owners who are accountable for cutover decisions. Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Readiness & CCoE

Migration Readiness Assessment

  • Business alignment and sponsorship
  • People skills and training plans
  • Process maturity for deployment and incident response
  • Platform and security posture
Action
Score each pillar and produce a prioritized remediation list that feeds the migration plan.

Cloud Center of Excellence (CCoE)

The CCoE sets patterns for security, cost governance, and operations. It runs pilot projects, updates runbooks, and builds training so teams adopt cloud best practices consistently.

Practical role
Provide templates for monitoring, backups, and rollback so each migration wave follows repeatable steps.
Misconception
Assuming a single training session is enough; continuous enablement is required as teams adopt new tools and processes.

screens.title: Phased migration planning and wave definition
screens.narratorSegment: Phased migration reduces risk by moving groups of applications in controlled waves. A typical wave starts with low-risk, low-criticality systems to build experience, then progresses to more complex, business-critical applications. Each wave should have clear success criteria — for example, less than X percent error rate, acceptable performance metrics, and validated backups. Rollback procedures must be documented and rehearsed. Use dependency maps from discovery to avoid splitting tightly coupled systems across separate waves. A common misconception is planning waves only by system criticality; instead combine criticality with dependency and team readiness to form safe groupings. Example wave sequence: migrate file shares and low-traffic internal apps first, then move frontends with autoscaling, and finally tackle integrated backend databases with thorough testing windows. Also include dry runs in non-production environments to validate the cutover process. Key takeaway: well-defined waves and rollback plans turn migration into predictable operations rather than risky one-off events. What acceptance criteria should your first wave include? Phased migration planning and wave definition means group by dependency and readiness, set measurable success criteria, and rehearse rollback procedures to reduce risk.. In practical terms, define waves, success criteria, and rollback procedures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Phased Planning

Wave definition steps

  1. Use dependency maps to form candidate groups.
  2. Score groups by criticality and readiness.
  3. Define success criteria and rollback procedures for the group.
  4. Rehearse the cutover in non-production and document lessons learned.
Example wave plan
Wave 1: Internal file shares (low risk). Wave 2: Customer-facing frontend (scale tests). Wave 3: Backend databases (coordinated cutover).

Success criteria checklist

  • Performance within X% of baseline.
  • All integration tests pass.
  • Backups verified and restore tested.
  • Stakeholder sign-off and documented rollback steps.
Key Takeaway

Define waves using dependency data, rehearse cutovers, and set measurable acceptance criteria for each wave.

screens.title: Testing, backups, and rollback strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Testing and rollback planning are the safety net of any migration. Before cutover, validate backups and practice restores to ensure data integrity. Perform dry runs in staging that mimic production loads where possible. Define rollback triggers clearly — for example, error rates, failed integration tests, or unacceptable latency — and ensure automated or manual rollback steps are well documented. Another useful approach is blue-green or canary deployments for systems that support it, which minimizes customer impact while enabling rapid rollback. A common misconception is that backups alone are sufficient; without tested restores and verified consistency, backups may fail to deliver. Example: a database migration should include point-in-time recovery testing and validation against application-level transactions. Key takeaway: a tested rollback plan and rehearsed restores turn uncertain cutovers into controlled operations. What rollback trigger will you set for your next migration wave? Testing, backups, and rollback strategies means test backups, rehearse restores, and set clear rollback triggers so you can respond quickly and confidently during cutover.. In practical terms, reduce cutover risk through rehearsal and clear rollback plans. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Testing & Rollback

Validation steps

  • Verify backups and rehearse full restores in staging.
  • Conduct load and integration tests that mimic production traffic.
  • Define and document rollback triggers and exact steps to revert.
Best practice
Use blue-green or canary patterns when possible to reduce risk and enable fast rollback with minimal impact.
Sample acceptance tests
# Acceptance checks (conceptual)
- All integration tests pass against migrated systems
- Error rate < 0.5% over 10 minutes
- Latency remains within defined SLA
- Backups completed and a point-in-time restore verified
Without rehearsed restores and clear rollback criteria, teams face long outages during unexpected failures. Build checklists and rehearse until the team can execute confidently under time pressure.

screens.title: Activity: Migration Strategy Decision Matrix
screens.narratorSegment: This activity asks you to choose the most suitable R strategy for three applications and justify the choice. Use the characteristics and business goals to balance risk, cost, and available teams. For Application 1, a legacy HR system that is critical, rarely updated, tightly integrated with on-premises directory, uses an old Oracle database, and lacks a dev team, the most pragmatic choice is Rehost: preserve functionality, reduce hardware cost, and avoid risky refactoring. For Application 2, a customer-facing e-commerce frontend with high traffic variability and an existing DevOps team, Replatform or Refactor are both viable; Replatform is often the practical next step: move to managed services and autoscaling to improve scalability quickly, then plan refactor for long-term agility. For Application 3, an internal low-usage file share server needs minimal features and aims to reduce maintenance — Repurchase or Retire apply; moving to a managed file service or SaaS file store (Repurchase) eliminates the server. Common misconception: choosing refactor for every public-facing system; refactoring demands time and should match roadmap value. Key takeaway: justify each R with technical and business evidence and name a central AWS approach for implementation.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Decision Matrix Activity

Applications

Application 1: Legacy HR System
Critical, rarely updated, tightly coupled to on-prem directory, Oracle DB, no dev team.
Application 2: E-commerce Frontend
High traffic variability, frequent updates, Apache/PHP, MySQL, DevOps team present.
Application 3: Internal File Share
Low usage, simple access needs, SMB share on Windows Server.

Suggested decisions

Application 1:
Chosen R-Strategy: Rehost
Justification: Critical and tightly coupled; minimize risk and reduce hardware costs without refactor effort.
Key AWS Approach: Use server replication and migration service to lift-and-shift with minimal downtime.

Application 2:
Chosen R-Strategy: Replatform (with a plan to Refactor later)
Justification: Needs scalability and frequent updates; existing DevOps team can adopt managed services quickly.
Key AWS Approach: Move to managed compute with autoscaling and managed database services for immediate gains.

Application 3:
Chosen R-Strategy: Repurchase
Justification: Low usage and simple needs; a managed file service removes maintenance burden.
Key AWS Approach: Replace SMB server with a managed file or collaboration service and migrate content.
After choosing, record acceptance criteria and a timeline for any follow-up refactor or governance reviews.

fullNarratorScript:
We begin by framing why careful planning matters when moving systems to the cloud. A migration is not just copying servers; it is an opportunity to reduce long-term costs, improve agility, and remove technical debt. In this lesson you will learn how to discover and inventory an on-premises portfolio, run a meaningful total cost of ownership analysis, and choose the right migration approach using the six Rs: Rehost, Replatform, Refactor, Repurchase, Retain, and Retire. You will also see how discovery data and dependency mapping supports realistic wave planning and risk mitigation. For example, a discovery report that shows heavy inter-server communication suggests grouping systems for a coordinated cutover to avoid runtime failures. A common misconception is that cloud migration always reduces license costs; in reality software licensing often follows vendor rules and must be evaluated separately. By the end you will be able to justify a migration using objective metrics, pick an appropriate R for each application, and draft a phased plan that aligns technical moves with organizational change management. How confident would you be to start mapping your own portfolio after this chapter?

These four objectives map to the decisive tasks you will carry out during a migration assessment. First, you will learn to evaluate existing environments and applications to determine migration readiness and complexity. That means inventorying software, servers, and dependencies and judging both technical and organizational constraints. Second, you will perform a Total Cost of Ownership analysis and construct a business case that includes both direct costs and often-missed factors like licensing, labor, and the cost of inaction. Third, you will apply the six Rs to categorize applications and choose the best migration pattern for each. This objective includes identifying when lift-and-shift is appropriate and when refactoring is worth the investment. Fourth, you will use discovery tools and dependency mapping to collect the data that makes planning realistic. Each objective emphasizes measurable outcomes: readiness scores, a quantified TCO, an R-strategy across the portfolio, and a discovery dataset that supports wave planning. Together these skills let you recommend a phased migration route that balances risk, budget, and business goals. Which objective will you try first when you return to your environment?

This second objectives slide connects each skill to a practical task you will perform. For readiness evaluation, you will produce an inventory and a complexity score that helps decide if an application is suited for lift-and-shift or needs redesign. In TCO work you will assemble a financial model that lists hardware, software licenses, power and cooling, labor, and potential cloud savings, and importantly show the cost of inaction as a sensitivity. For the six Rs you will practice writing a one-paragraph justification and a recommended AWS approach for each application. Finally, for discovery tooling you will run or interpret automated reports, use dependency maps to form migration waves, and use the data to set realistic success criteria. A common misconception is treating the migration plan as purely technical; in practice, every technical decision should map to business outcomes and measured success criteria. These practical skills let you move from analysis to an executable plan with stakeholders aligned and risks understood. Which task will you prioritize first in your environment?

A practical migration starts with portfolio discovery. Discovery is the process of identifying every application, its servers, databases, and the communication paths between them. You should gather configuration, utilization, and network dependency data so you can form groups of systems that must move together. For example, if an application server repeatedly communicates with a database server on nonstandard ports, those two should be in the same migration wave. Common tools automate collection of C P U, memory, disk, and open connections, which reduces manual inventory errors. A frequent misconception is that discovery only inventories servers; in reality useful discovery includes application owners, business criticality, and compliance constraints. This extra context often drives strategy choice: a high-compliance app may be retained temporarily. Practical steps include running automated collectors, validating discovered dependencies with app owners, and producing a dependency map that feeds wave planning. Example artifact: a CSV row per server with owner, role, resource utilization, and top outbound peers. Key takeaway: accurate discovery shrinks risk and shortens cutover windows. How will you verify dependency accuracy in your next discovery run? Portfolio Discovery: inventory and dependency mapping means inventory and dependency maps reveal grouping constraints and owner context that drive realistic waves and cutover plans.. In practical terms, collect the data that drives every migration decision. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Automated discovery tools collect a set of configuration and runtime metrics that are essential for planning. Typical data includes hardware configuration, installed software, C P U and memory utilization, disk usage patterns, and open network connections between hosts. The value of each metric lies in planning and risk reduction: utilization metrics determine right-sizing estimates for cloud instances, while network peers reveal groups that must move together to prevent runtime failures. The chapter references AWS Application Discovery Service and third-party tools as sources of automated collection. Use discovery to answer concrete questions: which servers communicate most often, which servers have single points of failure, and which systems have compliance constraints that prevent immediate migration. A common misconception is relying only on peak utilization; instead use typical and 95th-percentile metrics to size cloud resources practically. Example action: export a dependency map and mark nodes that require synchronous cutover. Final takeaway: discovery transforms assumptions into measurable evidence. How will you use utilization and peer data to shape a safe migration wave? AWS discovery tooling and what to collect means cpu, memory, disk, installed software, network peers, and ownership data are minimums for realistic migration planning.. In practical terms, what automated discovery gathers and why each metric matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Total Cost of Ownership is a structured way to compare on-premises costs to the cloud across the lifecycle of systems. TCO goes beyond hardware price tags to include power, cooling, datacenter space, software licensing, operational labor for patching and backups, and real estate. When you prepare a TCO for migration, include OpEx versus CapEx shifts and quantify the cost of inaction — missed opportunities that accrue when teams cannot move fast. A common pitfall is failing to capture labor accurately: on-premises labor for routine maintenance often drops when using managed cloud services, but cloud labor shifts toward automation and platform work that still requires skilled staff. Another pitfall is assuming licensing always falls with migration; many vendors require BYOL or new terms. A practical example: move a self-managed database to a managed database service to reduce patching labor, yet account for potential licensing changes. Key takeaway: document assumptions and run sensitivity scenarios so stakeholders see the range of outcomes rather than a single point estimate. What assumption in your current budget would change the most in a cloud model? Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) means include direct costs, operational labor, licensing, and the cost of inaction; run sensitivity scenarios against key assumptions.. In practical terms, a holistic financial view beyond hardware sticker price. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The six Rs provide a structured vocabulary to decide what to do with each application. Rehost is the lift-and-shift move where systems are moved as-is, often using server replication tools. Replatform involves small optimizations, like moving a self-managed database to a managed database service, without changing the application core. Refactor or re-architect means redesigning the app, perhaps into microservices or serverless, to fully leverage cloud services. Repurchase is replacing an application with a SaaS solution. Retain means leaving applications on-premises for now due to compliance, hardware dependencies, or cost reasons. Retire removes unused applications to reduce scope. A frequent misconception is treating these as strictly exclusive; in practice an application can move through multiple Rs over time — for example, rehost first, then refactor later. Concrete example: a legacy payroll app with strict compliance and no dev team is often rehosted initially, then replatformed or refactored in a later phase. Key takeaway: choose the R that balances risk, cost, and business urgency, and document the rationale so waves are defensible. Which application in your portfolio might follow a stepwise R progression?

Rehosting is frequently the right short-term choice for legacy systems that are critical or lack maintainers. The idea is to move systems as-is to cloud compute with minimal application changes, preserving functionality while removing hardware dependency. A practical example is using server replication to produce a target server in the cloud and cut over when ready. AWS provides migration services that can replicate block-level data to speed this path. The primary advantages are speed and reduced immediate risk of introducing application bugs. The trade-offs are that you may carry inefficient architecture into the cloud and miss cloud-native benefits. A common misconception is that rehosting eliminates long-term costs immediately; in many cases you replace CapEx with cloud OpEx while still incurring licensing and maintenance. Best practice: pair rehosting with a medium-term plan to replatform or refactor high-value systems once teams have cloud experience. Key question: which systems are so urgent that a controlled rehost is the best first step? Replatform and refactor represent two levels of investment with different paybacks. Replatform, sometimes called lift-tinker-and-shift, means moving to the cloud while making small optimizations. An example is migrating a self-managed relational database to a managed database service, which reduces patching and operational overhead without changing the app. Refactor, however, means re-architecting the application to exploit cloud-native patterns like serverless functions or container orchestration. Refactoring delivers the highest agility and operational cost benefits but requires significant development effort and testing. A misconception is that refactoring always delivers immediate cost savings; often it delivers operational agility and feature velocity, with cost benefits appearing later. Choose replatform when lower risk and quicker outcomes are needed; choose refactor when the app's roadmap demands scalability or continuous delivery improvements. Example: an e-commerce frontend with bursty traffic may be replatformed onto autoscaling managed services, then refactored into microservices as the team invests in cloud-native engineering. Key takeaway: match investment to business value and capacity to change. Technical moves succeed only when people and processes are prepared. A Migration Readiness Assessment evaluates business, people, process, platform, security, and operations readiness for cloud adoption. A Cloud Center of Excellence, or CCoE, centralizes best practices, governance, and tooling. The CCoE provides templates, runbooks, and training so teams can operate in the cloud reliably. Organizational change management includes upskilling engineers, adjusting operational roles from infrastructure maintenance to platform engineering, and communicating cutover windows and rollback procedures to stakeholders. A common mistake is treating migration as a one-time project rather than a transformation that alters runbooks and responsibilities. Example: a monitoring runbook must be updated to use cloud-native alerts and logging; otherwise incident response degrades post-migration. Practical actions include establishing success criteria, training plans, and appointing application owners who are accountable for cutover decisions. Key takeaway: align technical migration waves with training and governance so the organization can sustain the new environment. What internal training will reduce your post-migration incidents? Phased migration reduces risk by moving groups of applications in controlled waves. A typical wave starts with low-risk, low-criticality systems to build experience, then progresses to more complex, business-critical applications. Each wave should have clear success criteria — for example, less than X percent error rate, acceptable performance metrics, and validated backups. Rollback procedures must be documented and rehearsed. Use dependency maps from discovery to avoid splitting tightly coupled systems across separate waves. A common misconception is planning waves only by system criticality; instead combine criticality with dependency and team readiness to form safe groupings. Example wave sequence: migrate file shares and low-traffic internal apps first, then move frontends with autoscaling, and finally tackle integrated backend databases with thorough testing windows. Also include dry runs in non-production environments to validate the cutover process. Key takeaway: well-defined waves and rollback plans turn migration into predictable operations rather than risky one-off events. What acceptance criteria should your first wave include? Testing and rollback planning are the safety net of any migration. Before cutover, validate backups and practice restores to ensure data integrity. Perform dry runs in staging that mimic production loads where possible. Define rollback triggers clearly — for example, error rates, failed integration tests, or unacceptable latency — and ensure automated or manual rollback steps are well documented. Another useful approach is blue-green or canary deployments for systems that support it, which minimizes customer impact while enabling rapid rollback. A common misconception is that backups alone are sufficient; without tested restores and verified consistency, backups may fail to deliver. Example: a database migration should include point-in-time recovery testing and validation against application-level transactions. Key takeaway: a tested rollback plan and rehearsed restores turn uncertain cutovers into controlled operations. What rollback trigger will you set for your next migration wave? This activity asks you to choose the most suitable R strategy for three applications and justify the choice. Use the characteristics and business goals to balance risk, cost, and available teams. For Application 1, a legacy HR system that is critical, rarely updated, tightly integrated with on-premises directory, uses an old Oracle database, and lacks a dev team, the most pragmatic choice is Rehost: preserve functionality, reduce hardware cost, and avoid risky refactoring. For Application 2, a customer-facing e-commerce frontend with high traffic variability and an existing DevOps team, Replatform or Refactor are both viable; Replatform is often the practical next step: move to managed services and autoscaling to improve scalability quickly, then plan refactor for long-term agility. For Application 3, an internal low-usage file share server needs minimal features and aims to reduce maintenance — Repurchase or Retire apply; moving to a managed file service or SaaS file store (Repurchase) eliminates the server. Common misconception: choosing refactor for every public-facing system; refactoring demands time and should match roadmap value. Key takeaway: justify each R with technical and business evidence and name a central AWS approach for implementation.

Third, discovery and dependency mapping reduce migration surprises by revealing grouping constraints and owner context; validated discovery feeds safer wave planning. A common error is rushing to a single R for a whole portfolio; instead treat each application individually, supported by discovery and TCO evidence.
